title: 2 Chronicles 15:1–7
context: The Spirit of God comes on Azariah son of Oded, who meets Asa returning from battle. He declares that the LORD is with Judah while they are with Him: if they seek Him, He will be found, but if they forsake Him, He will forsake them. He recalls a time when Israel was without the true God, a teaching priest, or law, yet when they turned to the LORD in distress, He was found by them. He urges Asa to be strong, for his work will be rewarded. This prophecy is not found in Kings.

verses.text: The Spirit of God came on Azariah the son of Oded.
verses.arminianNotes: The Spirit of God comes on Azariah son of Oded. Arminian readers see the Spirit empowering a prophet to speak God’s word at a key moment after victory, when encouragement and warning are needed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God taking the initiative to address His people through a prophet. Shared ground: both traditions read the Spirit’s coming as enabling a specific word, as with Amasai in 1 Chronicles 12:18.

verses.text: He went out to meet Asa, and said to him, “Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin! The LORD is with you while you are with him; and if you seek him, he will be found by you; but if you forsake him, he will forsake you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD is with Judah while they are with Him; if they seek Him, He will be found, but if they forsake Him, He will forsake them. Arminian readers see a real covenant condition; see the existing contrasts at Exodus 19:5 and 1 Samuel 12:22.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conditional as a means by which God calls and keeps His people, as those boxes explain. Shared ground: both traditions take the warning seriously and agree that seeking God is the path of blessing.

verses.text: Now for a long time Israel was without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without law.
verses.arminianNotes: For a long time Israel was without the true God, a teaching priest, or law. Arminian readers note that many read this as describing a period such as the judges, though the verse does not name a specific time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the description as a warning of what happens when God’s word is neglected. Both traditions note that the verse may also look ahead or speak generally, and they read it without fixing a single referent.

verses.text: But when in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him, he was found by them.
verses.arminianNotes: When in their distress they turned to the LORD and sought Him, He was found by them. Arminian readers note the echo of Deuteronomy 4:29, where seeking God with all the heart leads to finding Him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that God’s grace goes before any turning and makes it possible. The two traditions agree on the encouragement Azariah draws from the past; how seeking relates to grace is already set out in the Hebrews 11:6 box.

verses.text: In those times there was no peace to him who went out, nor to him who came in; but great troubles were on all the inhabitants of the lands.
verses.arminianNotes: In those times there was no peace for those going out or coming in, but great troubles on all the lands. Arminian readers note the vivid picture of insecurity in daily life when people turn from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the turmoil as God’s discipline on nations that abandoned Him. Both traditions read the verse as part of Azariah’s warning, showing the cost of forsaking the LORD.

verses.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
verses.arminianNotes: Nation was broken against nation and city against city, for God troubled them with adversity. Arminian readers note that the text attributes the turmoil to God as judgment, while the conflicts arise from human choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the phrase “God troubled them” as His sovereign rule even over wars between peoples. Both traditions take Azariah’s history lesson as sober warning, without a separate theological dispute over it.

verses.text: But you be strong! Don’t let your hands be slack, for your work will be rewarded.”
verses.arminianNotes: Azariah urges Asa to be strong and not let his hands be slack, for his work will be rewarded. Arminian readers see encouragement to persevere in reform, with real reward attached to faithful effort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promised reward as God’s gracious response to work He Himself strengthens. Both traditions read the exhortation as encouraging Asa to continue the reforms he had begun.
